extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Latin literature / Horace (annotated-edition readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Critical/annotated edition fragment of Horace's Satires (with translation and scholarly notes) giving textual variants, literary interpretation, and contextual explanation for lines and passages. Useful for close reading, textual criticism, and dating/classification of the poems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modelled upon Lucilius
rubrics_metrics.description: This Satire is modelled upon one by Lucilius, who in his third book had described a journey from Rome to Capua and thence to the Sicilian straits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use parallels with Lucilius to identify source-model relationships (e.g., the comparison of Sarmentus to a 'rhinoceros' and parallel disfiguring lines (82–85)). Scholars cited (Lejay, Fiske) demonstrate close dependence; look for verbal/imagistic echoes and structural correspondences between Lucilius and Horace when arguing literary debt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steer clear of political gossip (authorial stance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the mission of Maecenas was a political one, Horace steers clear of political gossip.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting Horace's account of political journeys or embassies, prioritize personal relations, anecdote, and character-sketch over extraction of partisan political detail. The text reads like diary-notes rather than political reportage; avoid over-reading political intent where Horace intentionally omits 'gossip'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diary‑like compilation technique
rubrics_metrics.description: The account reads like a compilation of scanty notes from a diary, and yet leaves a delightful impression about the personal relations of men distinguished in literature and statesmanship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and value fragmentary, episodic, or 'note-like' passages as a deliberate stylistic technique that can produce vivid personal portraiture. Do not mistake brevity or apparent incompleteness for poor composition—they can be an aesthetic choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mock‑heroic treatment in satiric scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Some characteristics of the sketch are doubtless due to Horace's adherence to the satiric type. Thus the encounter of the two buffoons (51–69) is a dramatic scene, treated in a mock-heroic fashion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing satiric passages, look for elevated diction, epic analogues, and mock-heroic tropes used to comic effect (e.g., treating a low or comic incident in grandiose terms). Use such registers to read Horace's satiric aims and effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify close dependence via parallel lines and incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: This close dependence of Horace upon Lucilius throughout is clearly shown both by Lejay... and by Fiske in his Lucilius and Horace, pp. 306 ff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish literary dependence by citing specific parallel incidents, images, or lines (noting line numbers where possible). Use scholarly concordances (Lejay, Fiske) as supporting authority. Parallelism at the level of concrete images (e.g., rhinoceros simile) is strong evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual emendation guided by metrical constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: The name Apollodorus cannot be used in hexameters, and Heliodorus would be an easy substitution for Apollo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing or evaluating emendations, consider whether a reading fits the metrically required form (hexameter scansion). Meter can justify substitution/conjecture of alternate names or forms; note when proposed identifications are motivated by metrical feasibility as well as historical plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use internal absence/presence of references for dating
rubrics_metrics.description: As this interesting Satire contains no allusion to the Sabine farm, it was probably composed before 33 B.C., the year when Maecenas presented him with the estate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Date poems by internal evidence: absence of an event or possession known to have occurred by a certain date can indicate composition before that date. Conversely, references to places, gifts, or personae can furnish terminus post quem/ante quem. State such dating cautiously and cite the relevant internal markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group poems by subject and treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: In its subject and treatment it is to be grouped with the third, fourth, and tenth Satires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify individual satires with others sharing thematic focus and mode (autobiographical defence, social/political ambition, personal relations). Use grouping to support arguments about development of themes across books and to contextualize individual poems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotate cultural and lexical references for modern readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes explain features such as colonnades/porticoes (used for promenading), the lectulus (easy couch), Market of Appius, Feronia, 'Atabulus' (hot scirocco), and local geography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide succinct explanatory notes for culturally specific terms, topography, institutions, and everyday objects to aid comprehension. When annotating, include classical references (Acts xxviii.15; Pliny) or etymological/contextual commentary as needed for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial practice: record manuscript variants and conjectures
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout the text footnotes record variant readings, conjectures, deletions by editors (e.g., 'Line 92 was deleted by Bentley', variant sigla CK, D, etc.), and alternative readings (incumbo/includo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In producing or using an edition, list manuscript variants and the editorial choices made (with sigla), and explain conjectural emendations and deletions. Justify editorial decisions by reference to manuscript authority, internal sense, metrical requirements, and precedent in scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret satiric purpose via autobiographical and moral themes
rubrics_metrics.description: This Satire... disclaims such ambition for himself, sets forth the principles upon which Maecenas chooses his friends, and pays a noble tribute to his oft father, to whom he is indebted for all that he is, both in character and education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing satiric intent, attend to autobiographical elements and moral argument: defensive posture against social envy, praise of patronage, and moral indebtedness to family. These thematic readings explain rhetorical choices and help situate the poem in Horace's larger project.
